Researchers investigating the life history of the goliath catfish Zungaro dorado have documented that newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from the egg envelope at a remarkably small size. The wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0028 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0028 grams], a value reflecting the modest yolk reserves packaged within the demersal egg. This initial mass is consistent with the general pattern observed among large migratory pimelodids, where neonates are relatively altricial. The subsequent yolk absorption period proceeds rapidly under the elevated thermal conditions characteristic of the Amazon basin. When incubated at a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time from fertilisation to chorion rupture is approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days], a brief developmental window that aligns with the species' preference for warm, slow-moving waters during the spawning season. This rapid embryonic development is likely an adaptation to high predation pressure on the incubating egg stage, favouring quick passage through the most vulnerable phase of the life cycle.

As the free-swimming larvae transition to exogenous feeding and enter the pelagic larval phase, they begin a period of sustained somatic growth that will ultimately determine their maximum attainable size. Field surveys and mark-recapture studies of adult specimens have established that the ultimate total length for this species reaches 192 centimetres [Li = 192 centimetres], a value that places Zungaro dorado among the largest freshwater fish in South America. Interestingly, a marked sexual dimorphism in maximum length is apparent, with males attaining a smaller ultimate total length of 173 centimetres [Li = 173 centimetres]. This disparity suggests that females may allocate a greater proportion of acquired resources to somatic growth, potentially as a strategy to maximise fecundity through increased abdominal volume. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for the largest individuals has been estimated at approximately 94,100 grams [Wwi = approximately 94,100 grams], a body mass that underscores the substantial energetic demands required to support such a large piscivorous predator throughout its extensive migratory life.

The onset of reproductive capability in Zungaro dorado is closely tied to the attainment of a critical body size, reflecting the strong selective pressure for females to reach a sufficient abdominal capacity before initiating vitellogenesis. Studies of gonad maturation indicate that the total length at puberty for females is 88.5 centimetres [Lp = 88.5 centimetres], while males mature at a slightly smaller length of 81.7 centimetres [Lp = 81.7 centimetres]. This pattern is typical of many teleosts where the larger sex delays maturity to achieve a higher reproductive output. The wet weight at puberty for individuals reaching these lengths has been calculated to be around 8,300 grams [Wwp = around 8,300 grams], a value that represents a substantial fraction of the ultimate adult body mass. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of mature females has been measured at 20% [GSI = 20%] under the prevailing thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This moderate index suggests an iteroparous reproductive strategy where energy is partitioned between current spawning and future survival.

The longevity of Zungaro dorado is a subject of considerable interest given the species' vulnerability to overfishing and its late maturation. Mark-recapture data and otolith analysis from long-term monitoring programs in the Amazon and Orinoco basins indicate that the maximum lifespan under natural conditions reaches approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] when maintained at a mean annual water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This lifespan is relatively extended for a tropical siluriform, reflecting the species' position as a long-lived, slow-growing apex predator. The combination of a late age at puberty — necessitating years of growth to reach the 88.5 centimetre [Lp = 88.5 centimetre] threshold — and a moderate reproductive output per spawning event renders the population particularly susceptible to exploitation of immature individuals. Understanding this temporal framework is essential for establishing effective management strategies, as the long generation time means that recovery from overfishing can span multiple decades.

From a comparative physiological perspective, the life-history strategy of Zungaro dorado aligns closely with that of other large-bodied, potamodromous pimelodids inhabiting the Neotropical lowlands. The species exhibits a classic trade-off between rapid early growth to escape gape-limited predators and a delayed investment in reproduction that allows the attainment of a large adult body size. The yolk-sac larva mass of 0.0028 grams [Wwb = 0.0028 grams] contrasts sharply with the 94,100 gram [Wwi = 94,100 gram] ultimate wet weight, representing a mass increase of over seven orders of magnitude during the life course. Such an extreme ontogenetic trajectory necessitates a prolonged growth period, explaining the approximately 15 year [am = approximately 15 year] lifespan recorded at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The gonadosomatic index of 20% [GSI = 20%] was recorded in females at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Ongoing studies are examining how seasonal flood pulses and prey availability modulate these life-history parameters across different sub-basins.
